blocks.text: Dear Ms. Hubbard:

We are glad to take on the funding policy study for Wells, Walsh and Martinez, and this letter records the terms so that both offices work from the same document. It states what we will study, who will do the work, the fee, and the standards we hold ourselves to. Please read it. If it matches your understanding, sign where shown and we will begin.
What We Will Study

A funding policy is the set of rules by which a plan is funded over time: the contribution it aims at each year, the way gains and losses are spread, and the margins it holds against experience that turns out worse than expected. Our study examines the policy the plan has in place today and measures how it behaves when the future does not cooperate.

We will carry the current policy forward under a range of economic and demographic outcomes and set out the choices open to the board if it decides to change course. We do not hand you a single answer dressed up as the only one. We show what each choice costs, what risk it carries, and where the trade-offs sit, so the board can decide with the numbers in front of it.

One discipline runs through everything we deliver. We keep three things apart: what the data show, what we have assumed because no one can measure the future, and what we conclude from the two. The report is built that way, section by section, so a reader can weigh each assumption on its own and see exactly which conclusions rest on it. The work is performed under the Actuarial Standards of Practice that govern a study of this kind, and the report will name the standards it relies on.
The study has four parts, and the report will document each of them:

items: The current funding policy and the plan provisions it serves, read as they are written today.
The participant and asset data your office provides, which we reconcile and rely upon, with that reliance stated plainly in the report.
A set of projections that carry the policy forward under several economic and demographic scenarios, so its behavior is shown and not merely asserted.
A written report and a workbook of supporting exhibits, arranged so that every figure can be traced back to its source.

blocks.text: The Data Behind the Study

A study of this kind is only as sound as the records under it. We will rely on the census and asset information your office provides, and we will reconcile it before we use it. We do not audit your data, and the report says so; what we do is check it for internal consistency and against the prior year, and document what we relied on. We will compare this year's census against last year's, member by member where it matters, and raise anything that has moved in a way we cannot explain. Where a record is unclear, we come back to you rather than guess at it.
Who Will Do the Work

Michelle Banks, an actuarial associate in our firm, will handle the data intake and the preliminary calculations, and she will be your day-to-day contact for the questions that come up as the work runs. David Sherman, a senior analyst, will build the projection workbook and document the data behind every exhibit. I will review the work and sign the report, and I carry the professional responsibility for the opinion it states. The division of labor keeps one person accountable for each part of the work, and it keeps the reliance on your data in the hands of the people closest to it.
Fee and Start

Our fee for the study is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}, covering the work described above, the written report, and the workbook of exhibits. If the scope changes in a way that matters, we will agree the change and any adjustment with you in writing before we do the added work. Subject to your signature on this letter, we will begin on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}, and our first step will be to request the census and asset records and confirm the plan provisions we are to study.
Invoicing and Payment

We invoice monthly for the prior month's work, and each invoice is due within thirty days of its date. If a question about an invoice comes up, tell us and we will settle it before it becomes a dispute.
Term and Termination

This agreement takes effect on the date you sign below and runs until we deliver the report and you have paid our final invoice for it. Either of us may end it earlier on written notice to the other. If it ends before the study is finished, you will owe us for the work done to that point, and we will hand over what we have in a form you can use.
Confidentiality

Everything you share with us stays confidential and is used only for this study. Access inside the firm is limited to the people named above and to anyone whose work on the projections requires it. We will not take your information outside the firm without your consent, unless the law or our professional standards compel it, and in that case we will let you know unless we are barred from doing so.
Limitation of Liability

Whatever the theory of the claim, in contract or in negligence, our total liability under this engagement is capped at the fees you pay us for it, except where our own fraud or willful misconduct is involved. Neither side will owe the other for indirect or consequential loss. Any claim must be brought within one year of the day we deliver the report.
Governing Law

The law of the state in which our office sits governs this agreement, set aside its conflict-of-laws rules. Should a disagreement arise, we will first put it to a conversation between people on each side who have the authority to resolve it, before either of us takes it further.

If this all matches what we discussed, sign both copies where indicated, keep one for your files, and send the other back to me. If any part of it reads differently from what you expected, call me first and we will straighten it out before you sign. We are glad to take this on, and it will have the care a funding decision of this size calls for.
Sincerely,

To: David Sherman
From: Michelle Banks
Re: Funding policy study for Wells, Walsh and Martinez
The objective

This memo lays out how we will run the {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} funding policy study through its opening weeks. The objective is plain: study the plan's current funding policy, project how it behaves under a range of scenarios, and write a report the board can act on. We build it the way we build every report, with the data first, the assumptions second, and our conclusions last.
Our client contact is Lisa Hubbard, Chief Operating Officer. Data requests and scheduling go through her office. Client-facing questions clear with me before they reach her.
The work, in sequence

The study breaks into four pieces of work. They overlap in places, but the data has to settle before the projections mean anything, so the order matters. Numbering them here so we are working from the same list:

items: Data intake. I gather the census and asset files from the client and log what comes in, checking each file over before it goes any further. Anything that does not look right gets flagged and asked about, not guessed at.
Provisions and policy. We confirm the plan provisions and the current funding policy as they are written today, so we are studying what the plan actually does and not a summary of it.

Projection workbook. David Sherman builds the model that carries the policy forward under the agreed scenarios, with every exhibit traceable to its source and a clean baseline run twice before any scenario work starts.
Report and exhibits. We draft the report and the supporting workbook together, keeping measurement, assumption, and conclusion in separate sections.

blocks.text: What we need from the client first
The study cannot start in earnest until the inputs are in hand. My first request to Lisa Hubbard's office covers three things:

items: The current participant census, with service and pay for the active members and benefit amounts for those already in pay.
The most recent asset statement, together with the custodian report it should tie to.
The plan document and the written funding policy as they stand today.

blocks.text: I will log what comes in and hand David Sherman a clean set to rebuild from. If a file is late or a field is missing, I will chase it down instead of working around it.
Who owns what

David Sherman owns the census rebuild, the workbook, and the tie-outs. I own the data intake, the client contact, and the first draft of the report. Where a record is unclear, we flag it and ask rather than guess.
Nothing goes to Lisa Hubbard's office as a question until we have checked it on our side first. That keeps our asks short and keeps her staff from chasing answers we could have found ourselves.
The opening steps
The engagement begins on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}, and the first stretch is all about getting clean inputs. Here is the order I will work in:

items: Request the census and asset files and log what we receive.
Reconcile the data against the prior year and note every open item.
Confirm the plan provisions and the current funding policy in writing.
Stand up the projection workbook once the data is settled.

blocks.text: I will circulate the reconciled file and an open-items list as soon as the data lands. Raise anything that looks off the moment you see it, rather than saving it for a status call.

To: Lisa Hubbard
Cc: David Sherman
Hi Lisa,

This message starts our working thread for the {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} funding policy study. From here on, let us keep the questions about data and assumptions in this one place, so nothing gets lost between inboxes and the whole team sees the same answers at once.

We are underway. David Sherman is reconciling the census file your team at Wells, Walsh and Martinez sent last week, and so far the head counts tie to last year's records. That is the sign we look for early, so it is a good start.

When you have a moment, we would appreciate two things: the most recent asset statement, and your confirmation that the plan provisions we were given still match the current document. Neither is pressing this week. I flag them now only because both feed the projections, and a clean set of inputs saves us a round of corrections later.

Once the census is settled, I will send a short summary of what we found: the counts, the covered payroll, and any records we had to resolve, with a note on how we resolved each. It runs to a page at most, and it gives your team a chance to catch anything before it reaches the model.
Please reply on this thread rather than to me alone.
Sincerely
Meeting Minutes: Funding Policy Study for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}

The data is closed, and the study has moved to the projections and the scenarios that sit on top of them. That was the substance of the session. The rest of the discussion was about which scenarios to run and how to present the range, not about the inputs, which are now settled.
Attendees

items: Michelle Banks, Actuarial Associate
David Sherman, Senior Analyst
Lisa Hubbard, Chief Operating Officer, Wells, Walsh and Martinez

blocks.text: Discussion

David Sherman took the group through the census, which is now reconciled and closed. The active and inactive counts tie to the prior file, the covered payroll ties as well, and the few records that came in without clean service dates were run down against the client's source data. We rely on the reconciled file from here forward, and the report will say so.

Most of the meeting was about the funding policy itself and how to test it. We agreed to carry the current policy forward under three economic scenarios and two demographic ones, holding the plan provisions fixed as written. The purpose is to show how the policy behaves, not to argue for a change; the exhibits will present the range and leave the weighing to the board.

We reviewed the assumptions that drive the projection. The discount rate, the mortality table, and the assumed pattern of new entrants carry the most weight, and we agreed to test each at the edges of a reasonable range rather than settle on a single point. The assumptions will be set out on their own in the report, apart from the results, so a reader can see each one and weigh it.

Lisa Hubbard asked how contribution volatility would read to the board, and requested that we show the year-to-year swing plainly rather than only the long-run average. We agreed. The workbook will carry a volatility exhibit alongside the funded-status projection, and the report will describe in plain terms what drives the swing.

We also discussed how much of the mechanics to put in front of the board. The sense of the room was to keep the body of the report readable and move the detailed exhibits to the workbook, so the board sees the shape of the choices without wading through the arithmetic behind them.

Lisa Hubbard confirmed that her office will send the final asset statement and a written confirmation of the plan provisions, and said the volatility framing would help her brief the board ahead of the formal presentation. We did not set a date for the next review; it will follow the first full scenario run.

Michelle Banks flagged the one item still open. The most recent asset statement has not yet tied to the custodian report; until it does, the projections carry the prior valuation's assets as a marked placeholder, and every draft exhibit is flagged accordingly.
Action items

rows: Reconcile the current asset statement to the custodian report
Confirm the scenario set and assumptions in writing
Provide the final asset statement and confirm the plan provisions

blocks.text: These minutes stand as the record of the session. Corrections should come to me within the week so the action list stays accurate.
Status Report: Funding Policy Study for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}

Prepared by Michelle Banks, Actuarial Associate, for the leadership of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}. This report covers the study at its midpoint. The work is where the plan called for it to be at this stage: the data is closed, the projection workbook is built, and the scenario runs have begun.
Summary
The study is on schedule and within the agreed scope. The participant and asset data is reconciled and closed, and the current funding policy and plan provisions are confirmed as written.

The projection workbook is built and checked, and the first scenario runs are complete and in review. What remains is the bulk of the scenario analysis and the drafting of the report and its exhibits.

Nothing to date has surprised us. The one open data item, noted below, is the sort we expected to work through at this stage, and we are handling it accordingly rather than letting it hold up the modeling.
Finished this period
Three things closed since the engagement began:

items: Data reconciliation. David Sherman rebuilt the census from the files your team at Wells, Walsh and Martinez provided and tied the head counts, the covered payroll, and the benefit amounts to the prior year. The handful of records that arrived without clean service dates were resolved against your source data. The reconciled file is now the basis for everything downstream, and the report will state that we relied on it.

Provisions and policy. We confirmed the plan provisions and the current funding policy as written, so the study measures what the plan actually does today rather than what a summary of it says. Where the written policy left a step to judgment, we noted it for the report instead of filling it in ourselves.

The projection model. The workbook that carries the policy forward is built and checked, with each exhibit traceable to its source. We ran the baseline twice from clean inputs and got the same numbers, which is the test we use before any scenario work begins.

blocks.text: The work ahead

The next stretch is the scenario analysis. We will run the current policy forward under the agreed economic and demographic scenarios and build the exhibits that show how the funded status and the contribution behave across the range.
A separate exhibit will show the year-to-year swing in the contribution, not only its long-run level, so the board can see the volatility the policy carries and not just its average cost.

After the scenarios, we draft the report. It keeps apart the three things that are easy to run together: what the data measure, what we have assumed, and what we conclude. The board will be able to see which conclusions rest on which assumptions, and weigh each one on its own.
Budget

The engagement is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}, and the work to date is tracking within it. Roughly half the fee is earned against the data work and the modeling now complete, which is where the study should sit at its midpoint.

We do not foresee a change to the fee. If the scope moves, for instance if the board asks for scenarios beyond the ones we agreed, we will raise it with you and size the added work before we take it on.
Schedule

The study sits at its midpoint, and the remaining work is the scenario analysis and the writing. That is the more predictable half of a study like this, because the inputs are settled and the method is set.
We are holding to the plan we set at the outset. If anything in the scenario runs changes that view, you will hear it from us promptly rather than at the next scheduled update.
Open items and risk

One data item is still open. The most recent asset statement has not yet tied to the custodian report, and until it does the projections carry the prior valuation's assets as a marked placeholder. We expect this to resolve shortly and do not think it will move the conclusions, but the draft exhibits stay flagged until it clears.

The scenario set is the other item to watch. The scenarios we agreed cover the range we think the board should see, but others can be added if you want them. That would extend the analysis, and we would size it with you first.
Neither item threatens the schedule as it stands. We will send the next update when the scenario runs are complete, with the first exhibits attached for your review.
